rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s preaching does not depend on opponents’ wealth or patronage; God sustains him and his companions.
rows.anchor: God is his patron and sufficient to sustain him and his companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an itself is the greatest sign and was sent to convey the truth conclusively.
rows.anchor: It has been sent to them so that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those demanding a sign of the promised doom should wait, as the Prophet is told to wait too.
rows.anchor: if they think that this sign is not enough and would like a sign of the promised doom, then they should wait and he too will wait

none: English translation of the verses only.
English translation of the verses only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account just narrated is Moses’ story; such past accounts show God’s treatment of messengers and their rivals and foreshadow the rivals’ fate.
rows.anchor: these important tales of the past are being narrated to the Prophet (sws) from which it becomes clear how God dealt with His messengers and their rivals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an preserves the intended portion of earlier messengers’ accounts and teachings, together with the guidance for Muhammad as the final Prophet.
rows.anchor: the portion of accounts of the previous messengers and their teachings that was meant to be preserved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage threatens those who evade the reminder: the burden is their punishment, which they undergo forever and each bears alone.
rows.anchor: will bear his own burden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zuruq is the plural of azraq, literally blue-eyed, and idiomatically describes terror because extreme fear makes eyes turn blue.
rows.anchor: as an idiom, it also refers to a person who is terrified

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect wording about the trumpet conveys the event’s horror: a great cataclysm comes, but its sound’s origin is unknown.
rows.anchor: a great cataclysm will ensue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People now feel no fear of Judgment and consider it improbable.
rows.anchor: today these people have absolutely no fear of the Day of Judgement. In the first place they think that it is improbable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People dismiss Judgment as remote, preferring worldly pleasure; when it arrives they whisper that their stay was brief.
rows.anchor: they ignore it thinking that life, then death, then barzakh and then the hereafter are such far off that there is no need to worry about it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At resurrection people will not remember their time in barzakh and will think they had just slept and awakened.
rows.anchor: people will have no awareness of their time in barzakh when they rise on the day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A life seems long while being lived but brief at death, especially one spent heedlessly; the true perception comes when reality appears.
rows.anchor: it seems like a dream from which one has woken up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amthal means better or superior and is sarcastic here: the speaker is the person regarded as most clever among them.
rows.anchor: the person considered the most clever and superior among them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some classical poets’ deception made Judgment seem baseless; Islahi omits the couplets because this delusion persists beyond the age of jāhiliyyah.
rows.anchor: I am intentionally abstaining from citing relevant couplets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nasf can mean uprooting, separating grain from chaff, turning something into straw or ash, and blowing it away.
rows.anchor: The word نسف means to uproot something, separate grain from chaff, make something into straw and ash and have it blown away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fa-yadharuhā refers to the earth, an obvious referent that can be left unstated; Fāṭir 35:45 provides another example.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the pronoun in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāʿ ṣafṣaf is barren, level land without elevations, depressions, vegetation, or trees; amt means high ground.
rows.anchor: refers to barren and flat land, which does not have any high or low surfaces, vegetation or trees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs, including intellectuals, thought mountains indestructible; the question about them mocked that belief when Judgment’s cataclysm was announced.
rows.anchor: ask the Prophet (sws) about the fate of mountains

rows.speaker: Zuhayr
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s wisdom poetry reportedly says that, aside from the firmly rooted mountains, nothing withstands time’s calamities.
rows.anchor: Zuhayr whose compositions belong to the category of wisdom poetry is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where ancient Arabs saw mountains as unconquerable, modern people see themselves as invincible and imagine conquering the universe, forgetting the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: today’s human beings regard themselves to be unconquerable and proudly think that very soon they will conquer the whole universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hams is a low, stifled whisper; people who reject God’s Messenger now will then follow a caller leading them to doom.
rows.anchor: a low and stifled sound like a whisper

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intercession exception is severed and refutes the Arabs’ claim that deities can intercede for their worshippers at will.
rows.anchor: refutes the claim of intercession of the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beneficial intercession needs God’s permission and approval of the speaker; other conceptions are baseless.
rows.anchor: the two conditions of intercession which can be beneficial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge encompasses everything and creatures cannot grasp it; therefore no one can add information to Him or intercede on that basis.
rows.anchor: God’s knowledge is all embracing. None else can grasp the extent of God’s knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnā means expressing humility and meekness, while ẓulm here means polytheism.
rows.anchor: to express humility and meekness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse rejects the idea that alleged intercessors can confidently coax God into granting their wishes.
rows.anchor: They could ask Him with full courage, confidence and insistence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names al-Ḥayy and al-Qayyūm counter the Arab polytheists’ image of God as an inactive household elder who delegated all responsibility; God oversees creatures and has not abandoned them to others.
rows.anchor: God is a living God Who is overseeing the matters of His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because ẓulm is left undefined, every form of polytheism is rejected; shirk includes subtle forms as well as idol worship and ruins the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: whatever form a person indulges in it will not be acceptable to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse resumes the reminder theme of 20:99–100 after the intervening Judgment warning, using a fresh introduction and more detail.
rows.anchor: This verse is coordinated to what is said earlier from where this subject was brought up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ẓulm and hadm occur together, ẓulm means failing to render others’ rights, while hadm means embezzling or extorting from them.
rows.anchor: When ﻇ%ﻠۡﻢ and   ﻫَﻀۡﻢ occur together

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous believer receives full reward without injustice or loss; being a believer means the deeds adhere to monotheism, since shirk nullifies them.
rows.anchor: The condition of being a believer shows that the person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealing the Qur’an in Arabic favors the Arabs and makes truth conclusive, removing their excuse that no messenger brought a book in their language.
rows.anchor: a great blessing of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an explains the consequences of evading it in varied ways through knowledge, reason, history, and signs within people and around them, leaving no ambiguity or excuse.
rows.anchor: not left any ambiguity in stating the consequences of evading it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose of the elaboration is to cultivate piety and God-consciousness.
rows.anchor: purpose of all this arrangement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls Abraham and Ishmael settling Arabia and uses an expression meaning to remind people again of an anecdote.
rows.anchor: inhabit the land of Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is the Prophet’s sole weapon against opponents; it guides him through hardship, reassures him, and answers their repeated challenges. The Prophet eagerly awaited revelation like a soldier waiting for supplies to face a large army.
rows.anchor: the sole weapon of the Prophet (sws) against the onslaughts of his rivals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He should not demand the Qur’an before its appointed gradual revelation is complete, since God knows its timing and wisdom; he should pray for increased knowledge.
rows.anchor: God fully knows the wisdom in the time span He has allocated for it

rows.speaker: Our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes say the Prophet hurried to acquire revelation while Gabriel recited it and was told to stop; Islahi accepts eagerness as natural.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have confined its meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAhd means imposing a responsibility on someone.
rows.anchor: impose a responsibility on someone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam’s haste illustrates the danger just raised for the Prophet; Moses’ haste also had bad results, so gradual preaching protects the community’s training from gaps Satan or Sāmirī could exploit.
rows.anchor: it was this hastiness that made Adam (sws) commit a mistake

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min qabl refers to the earlier Adam-and-Satan episode; past family history can guide present and future generations.
rows.anchor: the past episode of Adam (sws) and Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam’s forgetting was a transient lapse under impatience; emotions are natural but must be bounded by patience and resolve, since unrestrained haste endangers people and society.
rows.anchor: all emotions are part of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an describes human beings as hasty by nature, citing 21:37 and 17:11; haste benefits them only when controlled by patience and resolve.
rows.anchor: Haste is an emotion among others and it is found in human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although eagerness to receive revelation is natural, Islahi rejects it as the reason the Prophet was stopped; the wider context explains the warning.
rows.anchor: the whole matter will become evident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi points readers to 2:30–39 and 7:11–14 for the wisdom behind the directive, prostration, angels and jinn, and Satan’s arrogance; he also notes that previewing the relevant part of Adam’s story before narrating it aids coherence, as in the sleepers’ story (18:9).
rows.anchor: The wisdom behind this directive, the nature of prostration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s jealous refusal of prostration became a challenge to God: he claimed humans were unworthy of superiority and Paradise and that most would follow him; God granted respite while warning him and his followers of Hell. The passage warns Adam that Satan is the enemy who may drive him and his wife from Paradise.
rows.anchor: Not only did Satan refuse prostration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired assurances describe Paradise as free from weather hardship: hunger and shelter matter in cold, thirst and shade in heat.
rows.anchor: the hardships of cold nor of hot weather

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some readers think thirst should be paired with hunger and the sun’s heat with shelter as a more apt formulation.
rows.anchor: more apt to mention thirst with hunger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects that objection as showing a lack of literary flair for Arabic, whose literature uses these paired conditions to evoke hot and cold weather.
rows.anchor: this is the result of a deprivation of literary flair for Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan exploits Adam’s desire for eternal life and fear of expulsion, persuading him that the forbidden fruit guarantees permanent life and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: Though Satan had been expelled from Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s strongest attack comes disguised as friendship and well-wishing, presenting forbidden conduct as the route to social and cultural progress; Islahi sees this tactic in current times too.
rows.anchor: his most successful line of attack

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghawa means to go astray; eating the fruit exposed Adam and Eve, who lost their promised attire while seeking eternal life.
rows.anchor: The implication of the verse is that Adam (sws) was deceived by Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some readers reconcile 20:120 with 7:20 by reading the latter as saying Satan warned Adam might become kings rather than angels; Islahi rejects this reconciliation as unsound and rejects non-mutawātir readings, retaining the muṣḥaf reading.
rows.anchor: in the first place, this reconciliation is not very sound

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan used several inducements at different times, promising both angelic status and an eternal kingdom; 7:22’s gradual enticement explains how Adam was won over.
rows.anchor: In my view, the answer to this question is that Satan tried to entice Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ijtaba refers to God inspiring Adam to repent and teaching him repentance’s words, as compared with the accounts in 2:37 and 7:23.
rows.anchor: Then his Lord blessed him, graciously accepted his repentance and guided him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s law is to draw a remorseful person near and guide him; ʿalā carries the sense of mercy, while hadā points to guidance against Satan later.
rows.anchor: he once again received God’s mercy and guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes Christian original sin and the claim Adam was humanity’s father but not a prophet; its wording and reason indicate he was a prophet given a sharīʿah for his descendants.
rows.anchor: This verse also refutes the Christian belief of original sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier discussions explain the wisdom of Adam’s earthly trial against Satan; the address is to Adam and Satan as two groups, not Adam and Eve.
rows.anchor: the address is towards Adam (sws) and Satan in the capacity of two groups

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The groups must regard Satan as their enemy to regain Paradise; Islahi rejects reading the dual as Adam and Eve because the plural parallel, jamīʿan, and their natural love make enmity implausible.
rows.anchor: the natural relationship between Adam (sws) and Eve is not of enmity: it is of love
